§7.2.1.1 syntax: 'T1 { [INNER] | { LEFT | RIGHT | FULL } [OUTER] } JOIN T2 ON boolean_expression'; 'The words INNER and OUTER are optional in all forms. INNER is the default'. 'The ON clause is the most general kind of join condition: it takes a Boolean value expression of the same kind as is used in a WHERE clause.' 'A pair of rows from T1 and T2 match if the ON expression evaluates to true.'

§7.2.1.1: 'For each row R1 of T1, the joined table has a row for each row in T2 that satisfies the join condition with R1.' 'While JOIN ON produces all columns from T1 followed by all columns from T2, JOIN USING produces one output column for each of the listed column pairs'. The select list then chooses and orders output columns: join-orders-customers.sql l.5-8 selects o.id, c.full_name, o.status, o.placed_at.

§7.2.1.1 LEFT OUTER JOIN: 'First, an inner join is performed. Then, for each row in T1 that does not satisfy the join condition with any row in T2, a joined row is added with null values in columns of T2. Thus, the joined table always has at least one row for each row in T1.' SELECT ref: 'plus one copy of each row in the left-hand table for which there was no right-hand row that passed the join condition'.

§7.2.1.1 CROSS JOIN: 'For every possible combination of rows from T1 and T2 (i.e., a Cartesian product), the joined table will contain a row consisting of all columns in T1 followed by all columns in T2. If the tables have N and M rows respectively, the joined table will have N * M rows.' 'FROM T1 CROSS JOIN T2 is equivalent to FROM T1, T2.' seed.sql@stage-0: 12 orders x 5 customers = 60.

Planner/Optimizer: 'A given SQL query (and hence, a query tree) can be actually executed in a wide variety of different ways, each of which will produce the same set of results.' 'The three available join strategies are: nested loop join ... merge join ... hash join'. The lesson only says the diagram is not the execution steps; it names no algorithm (depth_notes respected).

issues.quote: Counting after such a join counts items, not orders, unless you group the rows back into one per order
issues.text: The counting tool the lesson has just shown is count(*). After grouping the joined rows by order, count(*) returns one number per order (that order's item rows: 2, 1, 2, ...), not 12; only the number of result rows equals the order count. 'Unless you group' therefore reads as 'group, and the count becomes the number of orders', which claim 22 does not support. Summary line 4 ('counting afterwards counts items, not orders, unless you group') repeats the same wording.
issues.fix: §6: replace the sentence with 'Counting after such a join counts items, not orders. Grouping the joined rows back into one row per order, which [[foundation.l1.sql-group-by]] shows how to do, gives 12 rows again.' Summary line 4: replace 'so counting afterwards counts items, not orders, unless you group' with 'so the joined rows count items, not orders, until you group them back into one row per order'.

issues.quote: A missing condition does the same when you list both tables as `FROM orders, customers` with no `WHERE` to link them; leaving `ON` out of an `INNER JOIN` or `LEFT JOIN` instead stops with an error.
issues.text: I had to re-read this sentence. It brings in a second way of naming two tables (a comma inside FROM) that no query in the lesson shows, and 'no WHERE to link them' hints that WHERE can link tables, which the lesson never explains. The main point (the row count explodes with no error) is already clear from the sentences before it, so this is a pause, not a block.
issues.fix: Split it into two sentences: 'Listing both tables as `FROM orders, customers` with no `WHERE` also pairs every order with every customer.' and 'Leaving `ON` out of an `INNER JOIN` or `LEFT JOIN` instead stops with an error.' Or drop the comma form entirely.

issues.quote: then shows what a one-to-many join does to a count.
issues.text: The prerequisite summary taught `order_items` as the many-to-many joining table between orders and products. Here joining `orders` to `order_items` is called a one-to-many, and no sentence says why. I could work it out from `i.order_id = o.id` (order_items holds the order's key, so it is the many side), but I had to stop to do so.
issues.fix: Add one sentence after 'The second query joins `order_items` instead': 'Each order has one or more rows in `order_items`, each holding that order's `id`, so `orders` to `order_items` is one-to-many.'
